speaker: Mabel
teaser: Forty years of shushing. Now the whole world whispers back.
hello: Mabel Shush. Forty years a school librarian. My whole career was telling people to be quiet.
And now, at last, the whole world has listened. Everyone whispers. Especially my grandchildren.

which_ear.say: Both the same, dear. Equally hopeless, I'm afraid.

onset.say: Slowly. Over years, like a library book nobody returns. Nothing sudden.

ringing.say: A faint hiss in both ears, mostly at bedtime. Like a radiator. It doesn't bother me much.
ringing.note: Mild hiss in both ears, at bedtime

red_flags.say: No pain, no drips, no dizzy spells. My ears are very well behaved. Unlike Year Nine.

noise.say: Noise? I ran a LIBRARY. The loudest thing in it was me. Shhh!
noise.note: No loud noise: a quiet library career

ear_history.say: Never. Not one infection, no operations, no accidents. Not even a paper cut on my ear.

family.say: My mother had an ear trumpet. She used to wave it at the vicar.

health.say: Blood pressure tablets, and a touch of arthritis in my shushing finger.

aids.say: Never. My daughter booked today. She says I'm loud AND wrong about what people said.

say: Restaurants. All that clatter, and every word turns to porridge.
And my grandchildren. Their little voices just vanish. I turn the telly up; my daughter turns it down.

right.caption: Mabel's RIGHT ear: a tidy canal, a pearly eardrum. Neat as a card catalogue.

left.caption: Mabel's LEFT ear: just as tidy. Not a speck of wax out of place.

decision_lines.fit: Fit! Slow, matching ears, no red flags, and she's missing the consonants. A classic first fitting.
decision_lines.refer: Refer for what? Slow over years, ears that match, healthy eardrums, no air-bone gap. No red flags.
decision_lines.today: Nothing sudden here. It crept in over years, like dust on the top shelf.
decision_lines.clear: No aids? Her high pitches sit near 60 dB. That's a real loss, and aids help.

why.prompt: Why is Mabel ready for hearing aids today?
options: A slow, matching loss in both ears, and no red flags.
Exactly! Gradual, even and safe to fit. That's the classic first fitting.
She's 74: everyone her age needs hearing aids.
Age decides nothing. Plenty of 74-year-olds hear fine. Her chart and her history decide.
Bone matched air, so any inner-ear loss is safe to fit.
No gap clears one red flag. Sudden, or one ear worse for no known reason? Still a doctor.
Hearing aids will switch off her ringing.
They often make ringing less noticeable, but no promises. She's fitted for her hearing.

debrief: A textbook first fitting: slow, matching, sloping down to the high pitches. No red flags, so fit.
Vowels are low and loud. Consonants like s, f and th are high and soft. She misses those.
Family tips: face her, get her attention first, pick a quiet table, and turn on TV subtitles.
Restaurants, grandchildren, the telly: those are Mabel's goals. We check each one at her follow-up.
goodbye: Oh my. I can hear my cardigan rustle. Was the world always this NOISY?
Wear them all day. Your brain needs a few weeks to relearn the high pitches.
Quiet please, everyone. Mabel can hear you now.

headlines.S: SHUSH! LIBRARIAN HEARS EVERY WHISPER AGAIN
headlines.A: MABEL CHECKS OUT HEARING AIDS, NO LATE FEES
headlines.B: LIBRARIAN FITTED; A FEW STAMPS OVERDUE

subheads.S: A slow, matching, sloping loss and no red flags: a textbook first fitting, charted cleanly.
subheads.A: Gradual, even and safe to fit. The grandchildren's consonants are back on the shelf.
subheads.B: The right call, though a few stamps wandered. Check every tone in both ears.
subheads.C: High pitches carry the consonants, so chart every one of them, right up to 8k.
subheads.Do-over: A slow, matching loss with no red flags means fit. Mabel will be back, quietly.
